misconceptions.statement: Valency of an atom is the number of electrons in its outermost shell, always.
misconceptions.why: Valency is first taught using valence electrons for the first few elements, so students treat both as the same.
misconceptions.fix: Valency is the number of electrons an atom loses, gains or shares. It equals the outer electrons for metals like Na (1) but is 8 minus outer electrons for non-metals like Cl (valency 1, with 7 outer electrons).

probe.question: Chlorine has 7 electrons in its outermost shell. What is its valency?

misconceptions.root_belief: two related terms mean the same thing
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of student confusion between valency and valence electrons in chemistry education research

misconceptions.statement: Elements in the same period have the same number of valence electrons.
misconceptions.why: Students mix up rows and columns of the periodic table and remember only that 'same position' means similar.
misconceptions.fix: Elements in the same group (column) have the same number of valence electrons. Across a period the number increases by one each step.

probe.question: Do Na, Mg and Al have the same number of valence electrons since they are in the same period?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, all have the same valence electrons

misconceptions.root_belief: two related terms mean the same thing

misconceptions.statement: Atoms want to become stable because atoms have feelings and need to be happy or complete.
misconceptions.why: Textbooks and teachers say atoms 'want' or 'like' a full shell, so students read it as real desire.
misconceptions.fix: Atoms do not want anything. Arrangements with full outer shells have lower energy and are more stable, so atoms lose, gain or share electrons to reach them.

probe.question: Why does a sodium atom lose an electron?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the sodium atom wants to be complete and happy

misconceptions.root_belief: non-living things act with wants and purposes
misconceptions.source_hint: research on anthropomorphic and teleological explanations of bonding in chemistry education

misconceptions.statement: The octet rule means every atom must have 8 electrons in its outer shell, including hydrogen.
misconceptions.why: Students overapply the rule 8 because it is stressed so much, ignoring the duet for first shell.
misconceptions.fix: The first shell holds only 2 electrons, so hydrogen and helium are stable with 2 (duet). Hydrogen shares one pair in H2 and never has 8.

probe.question: How many electrons does each hydrogen atom have around it in an H2 molecule?

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from one case works everywhere
misconceptions.source_hint: studies on overgeneralisation of the octet rule in secondary chemistry

misconceptions.statement: Atoms form bonds only to fill the octet, so atoms with a full octet never take part in any bond or reaction.
misconceptions.why: The octet is presented as the sole cause of bonding, so students think it is the single reason for everything.
misconceptions.fix: Octet filling is a useful rule for Class 9/10 explaining why atoms bond. Noble gases are mostly unreactive because their shells are already full.

probe.question: Na+ has 8 outer electrons. Can it still be part of a bond in NaCl?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it has a full octet so it cannot bond

misconceptions.root_belief: one event has one single cause

misconceptions.statement: When sodium loses an electron it becomes negatively charged.
misconceptions.why: Students think losing something makes the atom 'less', so they associate loss with negative.
misconceptions.fix: Losing a negative electron leaves more protons than electrons, so the atom becomes a positive ion.

probe.question: What charge does Na get after losing one electron?
probe.wrong_answer: Na- (negative)

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student reasoning about ion charge and electron loss

misconceptions.statement: The charge on an ion equals the number of protons it has or changes in the nucleus.
misconceptions.why: Students think that charge arises from changes in the nucleus rather than the electron count.
misconceptions.fix: Ion formation only changes the number of electrons; protons in the nucleus stay the same. Charge is protons minus electrons.

probe.question: When Mg becomes Mg2+, what changes in the atom?
probe.wrong_answer: Two protons are added or removed from its nucleus

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

misconceptions.statement: Chlorine atoms gain an electron and so become a neutral, stable Cl atom.
misconceptions.why: Students link 'stable' with 'neutral' and ignore the extra negative charge.
misconceptions.fix: A chlorine atom that gains an electron becomes a chloride ion Cl- with a negative charge; it is stable but not neutral.

probe.question: What is the charge on chlorine after it gains one electron to complete its octet?
probe.wrong_answer: Zero, it becomes neutral

misconceptions.root_belief: two related terms mean the same thing

misconceptions.statement: An ionic compound like NaCl is charged, because it contains charged ions.
misconceptions.why: Students see + and - ions and forget they cancel in the right ratio.
misconceptions.fix: Positive and negative charges are equal in total in an ionic compound, so the compound is neutral overall.

probe.question: Is a crystal of sodium chloride positively charged, negatively charged or neutral?
probe.wrong_answer: It is charged because it is made of ions

misconceptions.root_belief: whole has the properties of each part
misconceptions.source_hint: studies on student understanding of ionic compound neutrality

misconceptions.statement: A molecule of NaCl is one Na atom bonded to one Cl atom, like a small molecule.
misconceptions.why: The formula NaCl looks like a molecular formula such as HCl, and diagrams show a single pair.
misconceptions.fix: NaCl is a lattice of many Na+ and Cl- ions in a 1:1 ratio. The formula gives only the ratio, so it is a formula unit, not a molecule.

probe.question: How many atoms are in one molecule of NaCl?
probe.wrong_answer: 2, one sodium and one chlorine

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from one case works everywhere
misconceptions.source_hint: widely documented in research on students' molecular view of ionic solids

misconceptions.statement: Each sodium ion is bonded only to one chloride ion, its partner that got its electron.
misconceptions.why: The electron-transfer diagram shows one Na giving to one Cl, so students think of a fixed pair.
misconceptions.fix: Each Na+ is attracted equally to all the nearest Cl- ions around it, not just one; in NaCl each ion has six oppositely charged neighbours.

probe.question: Which chloride ion is the sodium ion attracted to in solid NaCl?
probe.wrong_answer: Only the one chlorine atom that took its electron

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
misconceptions.source_hint: research on students' pairwise 'partner' ion model in ionic bonding

misconceptions.statement: The ionic bond is a bond that exists only between the two atoms that transferred electrons.
misconceptions.why: Teaching ionic bonding as a transaction between two atoms leads to thinking of the bond as a link rather than a force.
misconceptions.fix: The ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions in all directions, not a directed link between two atoms.

probe.question: After Na gives an electron to Cl, is the Na+ ion bonded only to that Cl-?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, only to the Cl- that received its electron

misconceptions.root_belief: a bond is a physical link or rod
misconceptions.source_hint: research on students viewing ionic bonds as electron transfer events instead of forces

misconceptions.statement: In a covalent bond one atom donates its electrons to the other atom.
misconceptions.why: Students carry over the idea of transfer from ionic bonding to every bond.
misconceptions.fix: In a covalent bond two atoms share a pair of electrons, and both atoms count the shared pair towards their own octet.

probe.question: In H2, what happens to the electrons of the two H atoms?
probe.wrong_answer: One hydrogen gives its electron to the other

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from one case works everywhere
misconceptions.source_hint: studies on students conflating electron sharing with transfer

misconceptions.statement: Covalent bonds form between a metal and a non-metal, and ionic bonds between two non-metals.
misconceptions.why: Students reverse the rule or remember only 'metal' involved without the pattern.
misconceptions.fix: Ionic bonds usually form between a metal and a non-metal. Covalent bonds form between two non-metal atoms.

probe.question: Which kind of bond is in CH4, formed by carbon and hydrogen?
probe.wrong_answer: Ionic bond

misconceptions.root_belief: two related terms mean the same thing

misconceptions.statement: A double bond means two atoms are bonded by two separate single bonds of the same kind in different places, so O2 has four electrons shared in total only if it is a triple bond.
misconceptions.why: Students are unsure about counting shared electrons and think the number of bonds equals the number of electrons.
misconceptions.fix: A double bond is two shared pairs, so four electrons are shared. O2 has a double bond, N2 has a triple bond (six shared electrons).

probe.question: How many electrons are shared between the two oxygen atoms in O2?
probe.wrong_answer: 2, one from each oxygen

misconceptions.root_belief: count the items, not the pairs

misconceptions.statement: Melting a covalent compound like water breaks the covalent bonds between H and O.
misconceptions.why: Students treat 'bond' as one thing and do not separate bonds within a molecule from forces between molecules.
misconceptions.fix: Melting or boiling a covalent substance only separates the molecules from each other against weak forces. The covalent bonds inside each molecule stay intact.

probe.question: When ice melts, which bonds are broken?
probe.wrong_answer: The bonds between hydrogen and oxygen in each molecule

misconceptions.root_belief: a physical change breaks the particles themselves
misconceptions.source_hint: research on intramolecular versus intermolecular forces in state changes

misconceptions.statement: Ionic compounds have high melting points because each molecule of the compound is very strongly bonded inside.
misconceptions.why: Students apply a molecular picture to ionic solids and explain with 'strong bonds in molecules'.
misconceptions.fix: Ionic compounds have high melting points because a huge amount of energy is needed to overcome the strong attraction between many ions in the lattice.

probe.question: Why does NaCl melt at about 800 degrees Celsius?
probe.wrong_answer: Each NaCl molecule is held by very strong bonds so it needs a lot of heat

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from one case works everywhere
misconceptions.source_hint: studies showing students explain ionic melting using molecules

misconceptions.statement: Covalent bonds are weaker than ionic bonds, so covalent compounds melt easily.
misconceptions.why: Students link weak melting resistance with weak bonding inside molecules, which is not the actual reason.
misconceptions.fix: Covalent bonds inside molecules are strong; covalent substances melt easily because the forces between separate molecules are weak.

probe.question: Why do covalent compounds usually have low melting points?
probe.wrong_answer: Because covalent bonds are weak

misconceptions.root_belief: one event has one single cause
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student reasoning about covalent substances' properties

misconceptions.statement: Solid sodium chloride conducts electricity because it contains charged ions.
misconceptions.why: Students notice ions are charged and assume charge means conduction anywhere.
misconceptions.fix: In solid NaCl the ions are fixed in the lattice and cannot move. It conducts only when molten or dissolved, when ions are free to move.

probe.question: Does a solid crystal of NaCl conduct electricity?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it has ions

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student ideas about conduction in ionic solids

misconceptions.statement: Ionic compounds conduct in water because electrons flow through the solution like in a metal wire.
misconceptions.why: Students know electric current in metals as electron flow and apply this everywhere.
misconceptions.fix: In molten or dissolved ionic compounds the current is carried by moving ions, not free electrons.

probe.question: What carries current in NaCl solution?
probe.wrong_answer: Free electrons moving through the water

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from one case works everywhere
misconceptions.source_hint: studies on electrolytic conduction as electron flow

misconceptions.statement: All covalent compounds are insulators, even when they react with water to form ions, such as HCl gas dissolved in water.
misconceptions.why: The rule 'covalent does not conduct' is memorised as absolute without exceptions.
misconceptions.fix: Most covalent compounds do not conduct, but some such as HCl form ions when dissolved in water and then conduct. Graphite, a covalent solid, also conducts.

probe.question: Will a solution of HCl in water conduct electricity, since HCl is covalent?
probe.wrong_answer: No, covalent compounds never conduct

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from one case works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: Covalent compounds always form separate small molecules, so diamond and silica have no strong network.
misconceptions.why: Students generalise 'covalent means small molecule' from water and methane.
misconceptions.fix: Most covalent substances are small molecules, but diamond is a giant network of carbon atoms joined by covalent bonds and has a very high melting point.

probe.question: Why does diamond have a very high melting point if it is covalent?
probe.wrong_answer: Diamond is not covalent, it must be ionic

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from one case works everywhere
